analysis.one_liner: Requires big drugmakers that settle federal fraud cases to fund FDA and NIH research.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Rep. Peter Welch with zero cosponsors, died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require very large drug manufacturers to pay a fee of 0.75% to 1.5% of their net income for each blockbuster drug that was built in whole or in part on federally funded research, but only if the company had settled a federal fraud or False Claims Act case of at least $1 million within the previous five years. The money would go to the FDA and NIH to fund medical research, and a company that failed to pay would see its drugs declared misbranded and barred from interstate commerce. The bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayer-funded medical research gains new money: the FDA would get funds for regulatory science, and the NIH would get funds for research on chronic and degenerative diseases that drive Medicare and Medicaid spending, on diseases with unmet treatment needs, and on early-career scientists. Patients ultimately benefit from that research pipeline. The bill also creates a direct financial penalty for big drug companies that settle federal fraud claims.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and NIH- and FDA-funded research

how_it_helps.text: Drug manufacturers with over $1 billion in net income that settled a covered federal fraud case must pay 0.75%-1.5% of net income for each covered blockbuster drug — a drug with $1 billion or more in annual sales developed in whole or in part through federal research — into a fund for FDA and NIH research.

Payments would be split between the FDA and NIH in proportion to their discretionary funding and would prioritize regulatory science, research on diseases that disproportionately drive federal health spending such as chronic and degenerative conditions, and grants to early-career scientists.

The payments must supplement, not replace, normal appropriations, and they cannot be distributed in a year when FDA or NIH appropriations fall below the prior year, so the new money cannot be used to justify cutting baseline research funding.
If a company does not pay the assessed amount, its covered blockbuster drug is declared misbranded and is barred from being introduced into interstate commerce, giving the requirement real teeth.

analysis.who_pays: Large pharmaceutical manufacturers that have settled federal fraud, False Claims Act, or FDA-violation cases within five years, and that have at least $1 billion in net income and at least one blockbuster drug built on federally funded research. The payment is multiplied by the number of covered blockbuster drugs they sell, so a company with several such drugs could owe a meaningful share of its profits. To the extent those costs are passed along, they could show up partly in drug prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big drugmakers with federal fraud settlements

drawbacks.text: The charge is multiplied by the number of covered blockbuster drugs a company sells, so a manufacturer with, say, ten such drugs and a $1 billion-plus settlement could owe up to 15% of its net income in a single year — critics would call that a punitive second penalty on top of the original settlement, and companies would likely argue it taxes drug development.
To the extent manufacturers treat the payment as a cost of doing business, some of it could be recovered through higher drug prices rather than absorbed by shareholders.

The misbranding enforcement mechanism is blunt: failing to remit a payment makes a company's blockbuster drugs illegal to sell in interstate commerce, which in a worst case could disrupt the supply of medicines patients rely on until the dispute is resolved.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real but modest: a new, protected stream of funding for FDA and NIH research, financed only by companies that have already settled serious federal fraud cases, with a supplement-not-supplant rule preventing budget raids. The costs fall on a small set of highly profitable manufacturers, though the multiplied-by-every-blockbuster formula is aggressive and some cost could leak into drug prices. On balance it is a targeted accountability-and-funding measure rather than a broad drug price reform, and its design could have been tightened before passage.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee on November 8 and 12, 2019, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter Welch (D-VT) introduced the Medical Innovation Act of 2019 on November 8, 2019.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors in the House.

It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and then to the Subcommittee on Health, where it sat with no further action recorded through the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large drug manufacturers that settle federal fraud cases — none of them was ever required to make the supplemental research payments, and the status quo for funding FDA and NIH research continued unchanged.

for.name: Rep. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee; it was his bill alone, with no cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Frank Pallone, D-NJ)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral without a hearing, markup, or vote; the record shows no action after the November 12, 2019 referral to the Health Subcommittee.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; the only recorded support was a single Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split was ever measured.

industries.note: The bill would directly charge companies with over $1 billion in net income that have settled federal fraud cases 0.75%-1.5% of net income per blockbuster drug built on federally funded research, with loss of the right to sell the drug in interstate commerce for nonpayment. Its interest in the bill ran against the public benefit of new research funding and a penalty on companies that settle fraud claims. In the end, the companies avoided the charge entirely because the bill never moved.

The bill would have created a supplemental funding stream for FDA regulatory science and NIH research on chronic disease, unmet needs, and early-career scientists, supplementing rather than replacing annual appropriations. This interest aligned with the public's and lost out when the bill died.
